opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that biology has historically been an incredibly empirical, artisanal science. We run an experiment, wait weeks or months, look at the result, form a new hypothesis, and do it again. That loop is slow and expensive, and it's a big part of why drug development takes so long and fails so often.

A virtual cell flips that. If you can build a model that has learned how cells actually behave, how they respond when you knock out a gene, add a drug, or push them toward a disease state, then you can run a lot of that hypothesis testing in silico first. You use the wet lab to validate and refine rather than to blindly search. That changes the economics of discovery.

Why now, and why by 2030? A few things are converging. We can now generate perturbation data at enormous scale: single-cell sequencing, pooled CRISPR screens, imaging, all getting cheaper and more multiplexed. On the modeling side, we've seen with language and with protein structure that when you have the right data and the right architectures, models start to generalize in surprising ways. And we have the compute to actually train on this stuff.

The analogy I like is that we've had models of molecules for a while, things like protein structure prediction, but cells are the fundamental unit of life. Disease happens at the level of cells and tissues, not individual proteins in isolation. So if you want AI to really move medicine, you have to model the cell.

To be clear, we're early. I think of it a bit like language models a few years before they got really good. The first versions will be imperfect and will predict some things well and others badly. But the important thing is that they'll improve with scale and with tight lab-in-the-loop feedback. Every experiment makes the model better, and a better model tells you which experiment to run next. That flywheel is what gets me excited about the next five years.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts existing models of molecules and protein structure with the need to model whole cells, which it calls the fundamental unit of life.

r002.rationale: The response discusses generating perturbation data at scale but does not propose a foundational dataset analogous to the Protein Data Bank.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to frame it is that biology has a prediction problem. If you take a cell and you perturb it, whether that's knocking out a gene, adding a drug, or changing its environment, we are remarkably bad at predicting what happens next. We can measure it after the fact with sequencing and imaging, and we've gotten incredibly good at measurement. But the forward model, the thing that lets you ask "what if" before you run the experiment, basically doesn't exist for most of biology.

And that's a strange place for a field to be in. Every other engineering discipline has simulators. If you want to design a bridge or a chip or an airplane wing, you don't build a thousand physical prototypes and see which one falls down. You run it in software first. Biology is still largely in the "build a thousand prototypes" regime, and the prototypes are slow, expensive, and noisy.

So the virtual cell, to me, is the idea that you can learn a model of cellular state and dynamics that's good enough to be useful as that simulator. And the reason it feels timely now rather than ten years ago is that the ingredients are finally coming together. The data side has changed completely. Single-cell methods, pooled CRISPR screens, large-scale imaging, these let you generate perturbation data at a scale that was unimaginable a decade ago, and that's exactly the kind of data you need, because you're trying to learn a causal model, not just a descriptive one. And on the modeling side, we've seen that large models trained on the right data can learn structure that's really hard to write down by hand. Protein structure was the proof point. Nobody hand-coded the physics into AlphaFold. It learned it from evolutionary data.

The cell is obviously a much harder problem. A protein is one molecule. A cell is tens of thousands of molecules interacting across time and space, with stochasticity and context dependence everywhere. So I'm not claiming that by 2030 we'll have a complete, mechanistic digital twin of a cell. I think that framing actually sets people up to be disappointed. What I think is realistic is a model that's predictive in the ways that matter for decisions. Can it tell you which perturbation is most likely to move a cell from a diseased state toward a healthy one? Can it tell you which experiment is most informative to run next? Can it tell you where it's uncertain, so you know where to go collect data?

And that last piece is actually the part I find most exciting, because it changes the relationship between the model and the lab. Right now the lab produces data and the model consumes it. In the version I'm describing, it's a loop. The model proposes, the lab tests, the model updates. And once you have automated experimentation on the wet side, that loop can run much faster than a human can run it. That's when the whole thing starts to compound.

So the reason I think it's the important direction is that it's the piece that connects everything else. Target discovery, drug design, understanding disease mechanism, cell engineering, all of those are downstream of being able to predict cellular behavior. If you can get even a moderately good virtual cell, every one of those problems gets easier at the same time. That's a pretty unusual kind of leverage, and I think it's worth a lot of the field's attention over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts protein structure prediction with the greater complexity of modeling a whole cell, but does not say the field predominantly focuses on proteins.

r002.rationale: It describes perturbation data as important for learning virtual-cell models, but does not propose a foundational dataset analogous to the Protein Data Bank.

astra-6.text:
I think virtual-cell models could change the basic loop of how we do biology. Today, we have an idea, we design an experiment, and then we wait to see what happens. Experiments are expensive, and the space of things we could try is enormous. Even a single cell has so many interacting components that it’s hard to reason about what happens when you change several of them at once.

The promise of a virtual cell is to make useful predictions about those changes. If I perturb this gene, introduce this combination of edits, or expose a cell to a drug, what happens? And how does that depend on the cell’s starting state? A model that can answer those questions reliably would help us choose much better experiments.

The key is moving beyond describing biological data toward predicting interventions. You can have a model that captures patterns beautifully and still fails when you ask it to predict something outside the conditions it has seen. So the experimental feedback loop is essential: make predictions, test them, and use the failures to improve the model.

By 2030, I’d be excited to see models that are genuinely useful within well-defined biological settings. They don’t have to simulate every molecule to matter. If they help us identify a therapeutic target or engineer a cell with substantially fewer rounds of trial and error, that’s a major change in how we discover and build things in biology.

r001.rationale: The response discusses modeling whole cells and predicting interventions, but it does not contrast this with a predominant focus on proteins.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose a foundational dataset or compare one to the Protein Data Bank.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a lot of biology today is still about running an experiment, seeing what happens, and then deciding what to try next. That loop is expensive and slow. A virtual-cell model could help us ask, before we do the experiment: If I perturb this gene, or introduce this drug, how might the cell respond?

The exciting thing is moving from recognizing patterns to predicting the consequences of interventions. And that’s a much harder problem. A cell has many interacting layers, and its response depends on its state and environment. A useful model needs to capture enough of that context to help us make better experimental decisions.

By 2030, I wouldn’t expect a perfect digital replica of a cell. But models that reliably guide experiments in particular settings could already be transformative. You could explore more hypotheses, prioritize the most informative experiments, and feed those results back into the model. That tighter loop between computation and experiment is what makes this direction so important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses modeling cellular responses and interacting layers, but does not say the field predominantly focuses on proteins or contrast that with modeling whole cells.

r002.rationale: It proposes no foundational dataset and makes no analogy to the Protein Data Bank enabling protein-structure prediction.
